US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.

It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".

Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.

Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.

It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as

the US national intelligence director

in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.

On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.

The announcement of the taskforce

follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.

"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.

Trump has

dismissed calls for stronger oversight

and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.

The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton

On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Some experts have

questioned the logic of the rebranding

, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.

Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.

"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.

The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.

Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a

public spat with Trump

review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Date: 2026-10-05T17:23:19+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent | Amazon Web Services
English normalization: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent | Amazon Web Services
Collected full article body: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent

Engineers increasingly use coding assistance tools to accelerate their development workflows. Today, Amazon SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference introduces the aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS. This skill gives coding agents like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex deep expertise in inference optimization and benchmarking. Install the skill, and your existing agent can benchmark endpoints, recommend deployment configurations, compare performance runs, and generate executable SageMaker Python SDK v3 code on your behalf. The aws-ai-ml skill is a toolkit that plugs into any coding agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP), turning it into a SageMaker AI inference optimization expert.

In this post, we walk through what the skill enables, how to set it up, and how it helps you move faster from model to production.

The challenge: Bridging intent and infrastructure

Amazon SageMaker AI supports serverful hosting across real-time, batch, and asynchronous modes. It offers on-demand and reserved capacity, heterogeneous instances, virtual private cloud (VPC) isolation, automatic scaling, and integration with every SageMaker AI training path. The surface area is broad and deep, but most engineers do not arrive knowing which instance family or serving container will best serve their needs. They arrive with a use case: a performance target they want to hit, a cost envelope they need to stay within, or a model they need to evaluate before committing to production.

The agentic experience for SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference closes this gap. You tell the agent what you want to accomplish, and it produces executable SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that you can review, modify, and run in your own environment. The agent asks targeted clarifying questions, generates code grounded in real benchmarks and measured performance data, and adapts to your business constraints the way a solutions architect would.

Throughout, you stay in control. Every step is visible in real time and expressed as code you can read and question. Nothing happens behind an opaque UI.

Getting started

You can install the aws-ai-ml skill through the Agent Toolkit for AWS on your local machine, or use it within an Amazon SageMaker Studio JupyterLab space. Either way, you can go from zero to a working conversation in 10 minutes.

Option A: Use with any coding agent (Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or any MCP-compatible agent)

Step 1: Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS. If you haven’t already, set up the Agent Toolkit. This requires AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) 2.35+ and uv installed.

This auto-detects your agents, installs skills, and configures the AWS MCP Server. For agent-specific setup (plugin install commands, MCP config), see the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting started guide.

Step 2: Install the aws-ai-ml skill. Add the SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference skill to your agent:

Step 3: Confirm and begin. Open your coding agent’s chat panel and ask: “What skills are available?” You should see aws-ai-ml listed. After you confirm, describe your intent in natural language. Your coding agent now has SageMaker AI inference optimization expertise built in.

Prerequisites: Your AWS credentials must have permissions to call SageMaker AI APIs (creating endpoints, running benchmark and recommendation jobs). The skill generates code that runs under your credentials. No additional AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) configuration is needed for the skill itself.

Note: For Kiro and Claude Code, agents can discover skills at runtime. They can search for and load skills on demand through the AWS MCP Server, without any local installation. Ask your agent: “Search for AWS skills related to databases.” Refer to the readme for discovering skills at runtime.

Option B: Use within Amazon SageMaker Studio

If you prefer to work inside a managed JupyterLab environment, you can use the skill in Amazon SageMaker Studio with a pre-configured image.

Step 1: Open Amazon SageMaker Studio. Navigate to Amazon SageMaker Studio in your target AWS account and AWS Region. Select your Studio domain and launch the Studio IDE from your user profile.

Step 2: Create a JupyterLab space. From the Studio landing page, choose JupyterLab, then choose Create JupyterLab space. Name the space (for example, my-inference-opt) and keep the sharing setting Private (skills only sync on private spaces). Under the Image menu, select the image that includes the SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference skill. This image ships pre-configured with the aws-ai-ml agent skill and all necessary dependencies. Choose Run space and wait for it to boot (5–10 minutes the first time).

Note: Use a fresh space. A reused space with a locally modified skill version may not pick up the pre-configured image.

Step 3: Open JupyterLab and launch a terminal. After the space boots, open JupyterLab and choose Terminal.

Step 4: Authorize your coding agent. In the terminal, authenticate with your coding agent using your identity provider. For example, with Kiro:

Step 5: Confirm and begin. Open your coding agent’s chat panel and ask: “What skills are available?” You should see aws-ai-ml listed. Once confirmed, describe your intent in natural language.

Troubleshooting:

If the agent reports no skills are available, verify that your space is set to Private. You can also check from the terminal:

If that directory is empty but /etc/sagemaker/skills/ contains the skill files, run restart-jupyter-server, refresh the page, and retry.

What you can do

The agentic experience covers the following capabilities across the inference optimization lifecycle. You don’t need to know which capability to invoke. Describe what you want, and your agent figures out the next step or asks clarifying questions if anything is unclear.

Benchmark an existing endpoint

If you already have a model deployed on a SageMaker AI endpoint, you can ask the agent to benchmark it. Tell the agent which endpoint you want to test, and it generates a Python notebook that runs a load test using the Workload.synthetic() and start_benchmark() APIs from the SageMaker Python SDK.

Before running any benchmark, the agent confirms that your endpoint is safe to load-test, because benchmarking drives real traffic to a live endpoint.

When the benchmark completes, you get a quantitative performance report with:

- Throughput: requests per second, output tokens per second.

- Latency: p50, p99, time-to-first-token, inter-token latency.

- Concurrency: number of simultaneous requests supported.

These are measured values from real load on real infrastructure, not estimates. The agent also recommends improvement mechanisms (such as prefill decoding) to boost performance.

Example prompt: “Benchmark my Llama endpoint on SageMaker AI.”

Find the right instance type for your model

If you have a model and need to find the right instance type to deploy it on SageMaker AI, tell your agent. It doesn’t matter where your model lives or how you obtained it:

- Fine-tuned or custom model in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3): You trained or downloaded a model and stored it in S3. Provide the S3 URI and your optimization goal. Example prompt: “I want to find the cheapest instance type to deploy my fine-tuned model on SageMaker.”

- Publicly available foundation model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: You want to deploy a foundation model (FM) from the JumpStart catalog then provide the model ID. Example prompt: “Find the best instance for model huggingface-reasoning-qwen3-8b on SageMaker AI.”

- Model on the Hugging Face Hub: You want to use a model hosted on Hugging Face. Provide the model name. For gated models (such as Llama variants), your agent surfaces the license terms and asks you to accept them and provide your Hugging Face token. Example prompt: “I want to deploy a Llama model from Hugging Face Hub. What’s the cheapest option?”

In every case, your agent generates code that evaluates your model against candidate instances and configurations, then presents ranked deployment options with concrete performance metrics: throughput, latency percentiles, time-to-first-token, and concurrency. You choose based on your cost and performance requirements.

Compare benchmark runs

If you ran multiple benchmarks (for example, before and after a configuration change, or across two instance types), you can ask the agent to compare them. Provide the two benchmark job names, and the agent generates a comparison that computes deltas across key metrics: throughput, latency percentiles, and time-to-first-token.

The results show percentage changes where positive means better, giving you a single, interpretable summary of whether your change improved performance, degraded it, or had no meaningful effect.

If one of the benchmark runs doesn’t exist, the agent offers to run it first before proceeding with the comparison.

Example prompt: “I have two benchmark runs and I want to compare them. Which one is faster?”

Benchmark results

This table compares two deployed models on the same benchmark workload (512/256 tokens, concurrency 4). The Δ% column shows how much faster Model B (Qwen3-8B) is than Model A (Qwen3-1.7B) on each metric. A positive value means Model B is better.

| Metric | Qwen3-1.7B (Model A) | Qwen3-8B (Model B) | Δ% |

| Output token throughput | 188.2 tokens/s | 271.2 tokens/s | +44.1% ✅ |

| Per-user throughput | 47.5 tokens/s | 69.4 tokens/s | +45.9% ✅ |

| Request throughput | 0.736 req/s | 1.08 req/s | +46.7% ✅ |

| Inter-token latency | 20.9 ms | 14 ms | +33.0% ✅ |

| Request latency | 5,382 ms | 3,658 ms | +32.0% ✅ |

| Time to first token | 67.5 ms | 166.3 ms | −146.5% ❌ |

The two models run on different hardware. Qwen3-8B uses a 4-GPU ml.g5.12xlarge (4x A10G), while Qwen3-1.7B uses a single L4 GPU (ml.g6.4xlarge). The deltas reflect approximately 4x the compute, not just the models themselves.

The takeaway: Qwen3-8B delivers approximately 44–47 percent higher throughput and lower end-to-end latency, largely thanks to the additional GPU compute. Qwen3-1.7B wins only on time-to-first-token, the expected advantage of a smaller model on a single GPU.

Putting it all together

You don’t need to memorize capability names or know which workflow to request. The following table shows how common requests map to outcomes.

| You say | What you get |

| “I already deployed a model and want to know how fast it is.” | Quantitative performance report: throughput, latency percentiles, concurrency metrics from real load. |

| “I have a model in S3 and I don’t know what instance to deploy on.” | Ranked deployment options with cost, throughput, and latency for each candidate configuration. |

| “I want to deploy a JumpStart model and find the cheapest instance. I only have the model ID.” | Ranked deployment options, no S3 staging required. Gated-model alternative surfaced if needed. |

| “I ran a benchmark before and after a change. Which one is faster?” | Percentage change across all metrics indicating improvement or regression. |

| “I want to optimize a Llama model from Hugging Face Hub.” | License surfaced, model staged to S3, then standard recommendation output. |

If your request spans multiple capabilities (for example, staging a Hugging Face model and then getting deployment recommendations), the agent chains them naturally within the same conversation.

What to expect from the agent

Your agent, equipped with the aws-ai-ml skill, follows a few behaviors that make the experience predictable and safe:

- It asks for what it needs. If information is missing (such as an endpoint name or S3 URI), the agent asks you to provide it rather than guessing.

- It confirms before impactful actions. Before running a benchmark that drives real traffic to a live endpoint, the agent warns you about the impact and asks for explicit confirmation.

- It tells you when something is out of scope. If you ask for something the agent can’t do (such as deploying a model), it explains what it can offer instead, such as generating the deployment configuration that you need.

- It generates SageMaker Python SDK v3 code. Every output is executable code you can inspect, modify, and run in your own environment.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:

- Delete SageMaker AI endpoints created during benchmarking or recommendations.

- Stop or delete your JupyterLab space if you used SageMaker Studio.

- Remove S3 objects stored by benchmark and recommendation jobs in your SageMaker AI default bucket.

Conclusion

The aws-ai-ml skill for Amazon SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference turns your existing coding agent into a SageMaker AI inference optimization expert. Whether you need to benchmark a live endpoint, find the cheapest instance for your model, compare configurations, or stage a Hugging Face model for evaluation, you describe what you want and your agent delivers measurable results.

To get started, install the skill through the Agent Toolkit for AWS and add it to the coding agent you already use, or launch a pre-configured JupyterLab space in Amazon SageMaker Studio. For more information, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

Original headline: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief
English normalization: The clock on AI regulation is ticking," warns UN rights chief
Collected full article body: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief

The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.

Speaking in the UK at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford on Monday, Mr. Türk said the technology could deliver dazzling advances in science, health, education – and even human rights work.

But its tools are being built and controlled by a select few, without public oversight, and are already doing things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.

Dystopia-creep

He warned that AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate in subtle ways, “letting dystopia creep in unnoticed”. Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services “at the click of a button”.

He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.

He also cited studies showing students who rely on AI retain less and think less independently, and asked whether the world is heading for a future in which no one can understand, question or even guide the technology.

As the UN rights chief was addressing the summit in the UK, New York City Council - home to the financial heart of the US economy - was also holding a rare Committee of the Whole to examine AI risks to New Yorkers.

The council is considering 10 bills to regulate AI across the nation's largest city, with testimony from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.

Mandatory safeguards

Mr. Türk called for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in how AI is developed and used, adapted as the technology evolves. Countries that host AI companies, or have influence over their supply chains, must require them to act responsibly and hold them to account when they do not, he said.

Not every answer lies in existing law and some areas will need new legal approaches, he added. But updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could offer protection in the meantime.

He also urged stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – “not in words, but in practice” – and a bigger say for civil society and people whose rights are affected.

“We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill,” he said.

Some momentum

Mr. Türk welcomed the creation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – both UN initiatives – along with a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the European Union.

He also said AI industry leaders had taken new steps last week on safeguards, self-regulation and risk assessment – apparently a reference to a voluntary accord signed at the White House on 29 September by President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies.

It carries no penalties for firms that ignore it, with President Trump describing it as “morally binding”.

‘Walk the talk’

“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.

“If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations,” he said.

review_queue.title: The Thélyson Orélien Case: Literary Criticism Tested by Artificial Intelligence
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: ina.fr
Date: 2026-10-07T08:29:48+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: Affaire Thélyson Orélien : la critique littéraire à l’épreuve de l’intelligence artificielle
English normalization: The Thélyson Orélien Case: Literary Criticism Tested by Artificial Intelligence
Collected full article body: Un « récit époustouflant », un « choc de lecture », une « langue à couper le souffle », un « rythme effréné » : pour Le Figaro, Mohammed Aïssaoui, critique littéraire et auteur, écrit deux papiers sur C’était ça ou mourir (Grasset), premier roman de Thélyson Orélien, un portrait de l’écrivain et un entretien. Par téléphone, le journaliste évoque son bouleversement, partage son « sentiment de [s]’être fait avoir », mais ne renie en rien ses écrits.

Les raisons de ce trouble ? Les révélations du compte (alors anonyme) Balance ton Claude, le 21 septembre 2026 sur X. Ce dernier l’affirme, sur la foi d’une évaluation du logiciel Pangram : C’était ça ou mourir résulte de l’utilisation d’une IA. La polémique enfle, le livre paru un mois auparavant (et Prix du roman Fnac 2026) devient un champ de bataille politico-culturel. En creux, elle interroge l’avenir du travail de critique littéraire dans un monde où des livres tout ou partie générés par une intelligence artificielle pourraient se retrouver sur les étals des libraires. Et duper les critiques littéraires.

« Un petit verre de Destop »

Journaliste à France Culture, Lucile Commeaux conçoit ainsi son travail : pas seulement comprendre « comment un livre a été écrit, mais se pencher sur sa réception, découvrir et décrire des écritures singulières ». Les rentrées littéraires foisonnent de livres qui se ressemblent, dit-elle. IA ou pas, cela ne changera pas grand-chose à son travail. Une position largement partagée par Tiphaine Samoyault, feuilletoniste au Monde. « Un de mes critères pour faire la critique d’un livre, c’est d’avoir quelque chose à en dire. » Lucile Commeaux et elle ne s’intéressent pas au livre à proprement parler, mais aux répercussions et aux débats provoqués par les accusations portées contre Thélyson Orélien — respectivement dans une chronique pour France Culture et une tribune pour Libération.

Dans « Le Masque et la Plume », Arnaud Viviant adopte une position nuancée et plus réservée que ses voisins de table, eux très positifs. Durant notre échange, le critique littéraire et psychanalyste s’agace : « On essaie de nous faire croire que la critique aurait avalé un petit verre de Destop, puis dit que c’était un châteauneuf du pape. » Il ne se voit pas comme un « juge de patinage artistique qui donne des notes » : dans le cadre de la rentrée littéraire, son rôle consiste selon lui à interroger les sujets des livres dans leur ensemble et ce qu’ils racontent.

Rythmes ternaires et phrases courtes

Une part des attaques les plus vives contre les journalistes littéraires pointe leur incapacité à reconnaître les traces supposées de l’IA dans le livre de Thélyson Orélien. Deux éléments reviennent dans les analyses. L’omniprésence de rythmes ternaires, d’abord — « un classique de la littérature française, » réplique Lise Wajeman, critique à Mediapart et professeure de littérature comparée à l’université Paris-Cité. Et la profusion de phrases courtes — « quand vous me parlez de ça, je pense à L’Étranger de Camus et ses phrases « sujet, verbe, complément et passé composé », avance Mohammed Aïssaoui. Je trouve ça facile de nous dire que c’était évident, après coup. »

Directrice de publication de La Nouvelle Quinzaine littéraire, Patricia De Pas reconnaît ne pas avoir non plus détecté un possible recours à l’IA dans C’était ça ou mourir. Mais elle estime, avec le recul, que des signes étaient là, et fait part d’une expérience antérieure : « Il y a deux ans, dans le cadre d’un de nos concours de nouvelles, nous avons reçu des textes aux styles très formatés, se souvient-elle. À l’évidence, il s’agissait d’une écriture automatisée. C’est difficile à expliquer mais tout sonnait faux. » Selon elle, cette affaire autour de C’était ça ou mourir va forcer les critiques à développer de nouveaux réflexes dans leur lecture.

« Je refuse de lire avec méfiance »

Mohammed Aïssaoui l’admet : s’il avait eu connaissance de l’utilisation possible d’une IA dans l’écriture de ce livre, il ne l’aurait pas lu. Mais il refuse de comptabiliser les répétitions dans un texte pour vérifier s’il a été touché par une machine. Cependant, depuis l’accusation contre Thélyson Orélien, le critique du Figaro l’admet : un soupçon s’est installé, furtif. « Dans les livres que j’ai lus ensuite, dès qu’un rythme ternaire apparaissait, je me demandais si je devais douter, admet-il. Mais je refuse de lire avec méfiance. »

Sa consœur Pauline Le Gall, critique pour Les Inrockuptibles, partage ce sentiment : « Je ne vais pas me mettre à douter systématiquement. Dans toutes les interviews que je fais, les autrices et auteurs expliquent à quel point ils aiment écrire. » La journaliste ne voit par ailleurs pas quel avantage stratégique les auteurs retireraient d’un recours à l’IA : même automatisée en partie, l’écriture d’un roman reste peu rémunératrice. Pauline Le Gall rejette par ailleurs l’idée d’utiliser des IA pour débusquer l’IA.

Pacte de lecture

Pour Lise Wajeman en revanche, le pacte de lecture, cet accord implicite entre un auteur et son lecteur sur la nature du texte (qui parle, dans quel but, s’agit-il de fiction ou non…) se trouve « profondément modifié » par cette possible artificialité. Reste à voir, selon elle, si le doute s’installe pour de bon. Elle estime, par ailleurs, que l’affaire C’était ça ou mourir pousse à réfléchir à la figure de l’auteur solitaire. Une construction somme toute récente dans l’histoire de la littérature. La plupart des journalistes littéraires interrogés s’accordent pour dire qu’un livre résulte d’une collaboration, a minima entre l’auteur et son éditeur. « Une simple discussion entre les deux peut changer la nature d’un manuscrit », analyse Mohammed Aïssaoui.

Lucile Commeaux voit dans cette polémique une rémanence des débats autour de la « littérature industrielle » du XIXe siècle — terme emprunté à un texte de Sainte-Beuve. À l’époque, explique-t-elle, « toute la presse conservatrice hurle à l’assassinat de la littérature » face à ces textes destinés à un public populaire, écrits par des auteurs parfois regroupés, payés au lance-pierre. « Ces livres ont toujours existé, ça n’est pas un problème en soi, c’est un autre type de lecture, tranche Lucile Commeaux. Par ailleurs, je me méfie du mépris pour ce type de littérature là. »

« Avec cette affaire, on se met à parler en statistiques, comme des intelligences artificielles, analyse Lise Wajeman, en référence aux résultats de Pangram. Un comportement qu’elle regrette. Je ne comprends pas pourquoi on accepte de se laisser imposer ces critères-là. »

Billet de blog

IA générative : les premiers changements du marché du travail sur les jeunes

Mise en ligne le

8 Octobre 2026

Auteurs :

Marco G. Palladino,

Antonin Bergeaud,

Antoine Bertheau,

Simon Bunel,

Oscar Degos

Billet de blog 463.

Depuis fin 2022, les embauches en CDI des jeunes ont davantage reculé dans les métiers dont les tâches peuvent le plus facilement être réalisées ou assistées par l’IA générative. Les fins de contrat diminuent également, tandis que l’emploi total des entreprises déclarant un usage intensif de l’IA ne s’écarte pas nettement de celui des autres entreprises. Les premiers changements observés passent ainsi davantage par les entrées et les sorties que par une baisse visible du nombre total de salariés.

Graphique 1 : Corrélation entre l’indice d’exposition à l’IA et l’usage effectif

Note : chaque bulle correspond à une famille d’activité française (FAP). En abscisse usage effectif de l'IA par métier d'après Google AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0 (avril 2026), mesuré comme la part des tâches O*NET du métier pour lesquelles un usage non négligeable de l'IA est observé, converti de la nomenclature américaine (SOC 2018) vers les familles professionnelles françaises (FAP 2009). En ordonnées l’indice d’exposition construit par les auteurs.

Source : Google Atlas, avril 2026 et indice d’exposition des auteurs.

Les recrutements réagissent avant l’emploi total

Les recrutements peuvent réagir à une transformation technologique avant que ses effets sur l’emploi total ne deviennent visibles. Une entreprise qui anticipe une baisse de ses besoins de travail peut limiter les nouvelles embauches ou ne pas remplacer certains départs, sans licencier les salariés déjà en poste. Cette marge d’ajustement est particulièrement pertinente en France où la rupture d’un CDI est davantage encadrée que dans plusieurs autres pays. Nous suivons donc séparément les embauches et les fins de contrat en CDI entre janvier 2019 et mars 2026.

Pour identifier les métiers où ces ajustements liés à l’IA générative sont les plus plausibles, nous construisons un indice d’exposition à partir du Répertoire opérationnel des métiers et des emplois de France Travail. Ce référentiel décrit plus de 1 500 métiers par les savoir-faire qu’ils mobilisent. Un modèle de langage évalue dans quelle mesure l’IA peut réaliser ou assister chacun de ces savoir-faire, en tenant compte de ce qui limite la substitution comme l’expertise tacite, la présence physique ou les interactions humaines. L’indice mesure une capacité technique potentielle et non l’usage effectif de l’IA par les entreprises. Toutefois, comme le montre le Graphique 1, la corrélation avec les données d’usage effectif de l’IA mesurées par Google Atlas est élevée.

Nous rapprochons ensuite cet indice des données administratives exhaustives sur les mouvements de main-d’œuvre et nous distinguons quatre groupes d’âge.

Le recul des embauches se concentre chez les plus jeunes

Une fois les métiers classés selon leur exposition à l’IA, l’écart apparaît nettement chez les 21-29 ans. En mars 2026, les embauches en CDI dans le quintile de métiers le plus exposé se situent environ 28 % sous leur niveau de novembre 2022, contre 8 % dans le quintile le moins exposé (Graphique 2). L’écart entre les deux trajectoires atteint ainsi une vingtaine de points de pourcentage. Il se réduit chez les 30-39 ans et les 40-49 ans, puis devient presque inexistant pour les salariés de 50 ans et plus (des résultats plus détaillés sont disponibles dans ce document de travail

Exposition des métiers à l’IA générative, adoption par les entreprises et dynamiques du marché du travail en France

).

Les fins de contrat évoluent dans le même sens, même si leur recul est moins marqué que celui des embauches. Chez les 21-29 ans, elles se situent environ 23 % sous leur niveau de novembre 2022 dans le quintile le plus exposé, contre 6 % dans le quintile le moins exposé. La baisse simultanée des entrées et des sorties correspond à une moindre rotation de la main-d’œuvre. Comme les embauches reculent davantage que les fins de contrat, le renouvellement des effectifs ralentit, surtout du côté des jeunes et dans les métiers les plus exposés.

Les premières études disponibles à l’étranger donnent toutefois une image encore contrastée. Aux États-Unis,

Brynjolfsson et al. (2026)

trouvent eux aussi une dégradation relative de l’emploi des jeunes dans les métiers exposés, principalement par une baisse des recrutements. En Norvège,

Hernæs et Kostøl (2026)

ne détectent en revanche pas de recul relatif du quintile le plus exposé lorsqu’ils considèrent l’ensemble des métiers des jeunes salariés. Au Danemark,

Humlum et Vestergaard (2026)

observent surtout une réorganisation rapide des tâches, sans effet moyen détectable sur les heures travaillées ou les revenus. Ces différences invitent à distinguer les métiers, les marges d’ajustement et les institutions plutôt qu’à rechercher dès maintenant un effet moyen unique de l’IA sur l’emploi.

Graphique 2 : Embauches en CDI des 21-29 ans selon l’exposition à l’IA

Note : chaque courbe correspond à un quintile d'exposition à l'IA des professions (310 codes PCS, sans pondération par l’emploi), du moins exposé (Q1) au plus exposé (Q5). Champ : embauches en CDI des 21-29 ans, hors entrées suivies d'une sortie du même établissement dans le mois, janvier 2019 – mars 2026. En ordonnées, l'écart relatif à novembre 2022 (trait vertical) de la tendance des embauches, en % : séries en logarithme, corrigées des variations saisonnières par effets fixes de mois estimés hors 2020, puis filtrées par Hodrick-Prescott bilatéral (λ = 1000).

Sources : déclarations de mouvements de main-d'œuvre (DMMO) et indice d'exposition des auteurs.

Les recrutements de jeunes reculent davantage dans les entreprises qui qui déclarent un usage intensif de l’IA

L’indice d’exposition mesure ce que l’IA pourrait techniquement réaliser dans un métier, alors que l’enquête de conjoncture de la Banque de France renseigne sur son usage déclaré par les entreprises. En appariant les deux sources, nous suivons environ 6 000 entreprises, dont près de 600 déclarent un usage intensif de l’IA début 2026. Ces dernières recrutaient déjà avant ChatGPT dans des métiers plus exposés, y compris à secteur donné. L’adoption de l’IA n’est donc pas répartie au hasard entre les entreprises et dépend en partie de la nature des emplois qu’elles mobilisaient auparavant.

Lorsque l’on classe les entreprises selon l’intensité d’usage de l’IA qu’elles déclarent début 2026 ( selon l’enquête décrite par

Genre et Parpais, 2026

), les embauches en CDI des 21-29 ans ont évolué moins favorablement depuis fin 2022 chez les entreprises utilisatrices intensives que chez les autres entreprises, tandis que l’écart est beaucoup moins net aux âges plus élevés (Graphique 3). Leur emploi total ne présente en revanche pas de divergence statistiquement nette. Au sein même des entreprises utilisatrices intensives, les recrutements diminuent également davantage dans les métiers les plus exposés. L’ajustement observé porte donc davantage sur la composition et le rythme des recrutements que sur une contraction déjà visible des effectifs totaux.

Coefficients en points de logarithme; les barres représentent les intervalles de confiance. Les groupes sont définis selon l’usage de l’IA déclaré début 2026, et non selon la date d’adoption. La diffusion de l’IA coïncide avec d’autres changements du marché du travail

Le recul des recrutements juniors dans les métiers exposés intervient toutefois dans une période où plusieurs forces ont touché les mêmes emplois. Le resserrement monétaire et la correction post-Covid du secteur technologique ont pesé sur les embauches à partir de 2022, notamment dans des professions elles-mêmes fortement exposées à l’IA. Le télétravail (qui aurait un effet négatif aussi sur le recrutement des juniors) complique encore l’interprétation, car il concerne largement les mêmes catégories d’emplois et a profondément modifié leur organisation. L’IA, le télétravail et le cycle de l’emploi ne constituent donc pas nécessairement des explications concurrentes, puisqu’ils peuvent avoir affecté conjointement les mêmes entreprises et les mêmes tâches.

L’enquête de la Banque de France mesure par ailleurs l’intensité d’usage de l’IA seulement au début de 2026, alors que les écarts de recrutement apparaissent plusieurs trimestres auparavant. Les entreprises qui déclarent alors un usage intensif peuvent avoir commencé à adopter l’IA plus tôt, mais elles peuvent aussi se distinguer par des caractéristiques qui expliquent à la fois leur trajectoire de recrutement et leur adoption ultérieure. La comparaison renseigne donc sur l’association entre adoption déclarée et évolution des embauches, sans permettre encore de séparer l’effet propre de l’IA de la sélection des entreprises qui l’adoptent.

Le ralentissement des embauches peut modifier les débuts de carrière

Le ralentissement des recrutements juniors peut avoir des effets bien au-delà du nombre d’emplois non créés aujourd’hui. En effet, plusieurs travaux théoriques récents montrent que l’automatisation des tâches confiées aux débutants peut réduire l’apprentissage par la pratique et, à terme, l’accumulation du capital humain de demain (e.g.,

Asriyan et al., 2026

;

Afrouzi et al., 2026

).

Nos résultats ne permettent pas d’établir que ce mécanisme est déjà à l’œuvre en France. Ils montrent toutefois que le recrutement des jeunes dans les métiers exposés, marge sur laquelle il pourrait apparaître en premier, a commencé à se contracter. Suivre seulement l’emploi total pourrait donc manquer une partie de l’ajustement si l’IA modifie d’abord le renouvellement des effectifs et la formation des travailleurs.

review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Baker Institute
Date: 2026-10-08T17:23:22+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: Artificial Intelligence and Healthcare’s Growing Data Economy
English normalization: Artificial Intelligence and Healthcare’s Growing Data Economy
Collected full article body: Table of Contents

Author(s)

Stephanie T. Schmidt

Nonresident Scholar; Founder and CEO, Health Wayfinder, Inc.

Share this Publication

- Print This Publication

- Cite This Publication Stephanie T. Schmidt and Heidi Russell, “Artificial Intelligence and Healthcare’s Growing Data Economy,” Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, October 8, 2026, https://doi.org/10.25613/Z3TE-5438. Copy Citation

Executive Summary

Americans now generate more health information outside the medical system than within it. As examples, wrist sensors record heart rhythms and sleep, applications track menstrual cycles and moods, and consumers order their own laboratory tests and describe their symptoms to conversational artificial intelligence (AI) tools. However, none of this health information is subject to the same protections as traditional medical information, like the records their physicians keep. Traditional medical information is protected by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA), which covers health information held by a particular set of actors, i.e., health plans, clearinghouses, providers who conduct billing or other standard transactions electronically, and their business associates. HIPAA’s boundary reflects a bygone reality in which medical data were stored in provider filing cabinets; accordingly, HIPAA is anchored on licensure and billing rather than on the data themselves.

Today, this creates failures both inside and outside the boundary of HIPAA:

- Inside: Tools that can help patients understand and use their medical information go undeployed because health system legal teams cannot say with confidence how they are classified.

- Outside: A fast-growing health data economy operates with no health-specific oversight, with enforcement occurring after the fact under consumer protection law.

Federal policy is actively enlarging the space beyond HIPAA’s boundary:

- Access rules move clinical records into consumer applications at national scale.

- The tax code now subsidizes data-collecting wearables.

- The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revised its guidance in January 2026 to exempt more physiologic trackers from device review.

This brief maps the boundary of the regulated healthcare space, examines what the boundary means for the development of new tools, the interpretation of health data, and the expectations of consumers, and in turn, recommends the following:

- The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) should issue definitive guidance classifying AI intermediaries that handle clinical data, with a safe and attestable pathway for patient-authorized tools.

- Congress should modernize the statutory definition of regulated health activity so that obligations follow the function performed and the sensitivity of the data rather than the identity of the biller.

- Federal agencies should formalize coordination between HHS and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) over consumer health data, and condition tax-subsidized purchases of data-collecting devices on plain-language disclosure of data practices.

- Texas should act on three fronts where it holds authority as regulator, purchaser, and funder: 1) clarify when AI interpretation of health data constitutes the practice of medicine, 2) set contract standards for AI tools in Medicaid managed care, and 3) fund accountable remote-monitoring programs in rural communities.

Regulated Space and Its Boundary

Imagine a patient in an emergency room. They are connected to a hospital heart monitor and are wearing a personal device that also records their heart rate. The monitor transmits to the hospital’s electronic health record, where the data are protected by HIPAA. The wearable transmits the same signal to a private application, where the data are governed by general consumer protection law enforced by the FTC. One person, one heartbeat, two regulatory regimes, two sets of incentives for innovation, and two AI training datasets, each holding an incomplete picture of the same patient.

The two regimes differ at every stage, from what triggers coverage to what happens after a breach, as detailed in Table 1. This brief is organized around two features of this comparison:

- Movement between the regimes runs in one direction: Once a copy of health information leaves a covered entity at the patient’s decision, that copy does not regain HIPAA protection.

- Who pays for a tool and who is accountable for it has a definite answer inside the boundary and a diffuse one outside it.

The sections that follow examine how the boundary is drawn, how the inside is enforced, how data cross the line, and what the growing economy outside it means for patients.

Table 1 — The Same Health Information Under Two Regulatory Regimes

HIPAA Regulation Follows Actors Rather Than Data

The HIPAA Privacy Rule applies to a defined set of actors, not to the health information itself. HIPAA’s privacy protections extend to “covered entities”: health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, such as billing, eligibility verification, claims status inquiries, and referral authorizations. It also applies to the business associates that serve them. Consumers largely do not recognize this distinction. In a survey of 2,000 U.S. adults, approximately 80% incorrectly assumed that health information collected by digital health applications is protected under HIPAA.

The regulation’s own definitions confirm that this boundary does not turn on what counts as healthcare. HIPAA’s regulations define “health care” expansively as “care, services, or supplies related to the health of an individual,” including any “assessment ... with respect to the physical or mental condition, or functional status, of an individual.” A definition this broad reaches well beyond licensed medicine to encompass:

- Wrist sensors assessing heart rhythm.

- Menstrual tracking applications.

- Unlicensed wellness coaches and Reiki practitioners.

- Grocery stores recording over-the-counter remedy purchases.

Yet HIPAA’s obligations attach to none of these unless the entity also exchanges health information electronically with a third-party payer or serves one that does. While the public hears the term “health provider” and assumes a uniform set of rules, the law distinguishes sharply between the licensed, billing-driven medical system and everything else.

Because a medical license functions as a state’s permission to practice and, in turn, to bill insurers, electronic billing serves as the practical foundation of the entire regulated space. Consequently, a licensed physician who accepts only cash and conducts no electronic transactions with insurers — not even eligibility checks — is not a covered entity. Conversely, a home monitoring device supplied through a physician or health plan falls inside the regulatory boundary, because its vendor is a business associate of a covered entity.

Payment Enforces the Boundary

The federal government has limited direct instruments for regulating hospitals and physicians. It relies on professional bodies and accredited medical schools for provider credentialing, and it influences care delivery largely through what the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) agrees to pay for. Compliance obligations accumulate as conditions of participation in federal programs, and commercial insurers frequently adopt the same standards because uniformity simplifies their own operations. The result is a regulatory space that is simultaneously overregulated in its procedural demands and underenforced in its substantive ones.

Limited federal oversight: The Office for Civil Rights (OCR) learns of HIPAA violations almost entirely through complaints and through breaches that regulated entities report about themselves — the federal government does not look for violations on its own. The one proactive instrument is the periodic audit program required by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act of 2009. It has run twice: a pilot in 2011–12, and a second round in 2016–17 that examined 207 organizations against eight of the 180 requirements in OCR’s own protocol, none of them the physical or technical safeguards that defend against cyberattacks. No further audits were initiated for seven years, and in November 2024 the HHS Office of Inspector General concluded that the program had not been effective at improving cybersecurity protections. OCR attributes the gap to resources, reporting fewer than 100 investigators nationwide. Detection, in other words, depends on the regulated entity or its patients coming forward.

Limited penalties: Direct penalties for violation of HIPAA are comparatively infrequent and modest in scale. The largest HIPAA enforcement settlement on record is $16 million, an amount unlikely to alter the behavior of a national insurer or large healthcare system. The precedent of hospital price transparency is instructive: When the cost of building compliance systems exceeded the applicable penalty, many hospitals elected to accept the penalty instead. Moreover, enforcement of that requirement obligated the federal government to develop a workforce capable of verifying whether posted prices were complete and accurate. What compliance does reliably generate is expense. HHS estimated that its proposed 2025 update to the Security Rule would cost regulated entities roughly $9 billion in its first year and $6 billion annually thereafter, and final action has since been deferred to at least 2027. In practice, the daily HIPAA compliance burden falls most heavily on staff, clinicians and trainees through annual training and incident reporting, while systemic exposure remains limited.

This raises a broader question: Why do hospitals comply at all? A large part of the answer is that compliance has become embedded in infrastructure. The HITECH Act paid hospitals to adopt certified electronic health records, and adoption rose from roughly one hospital in ten in 2008 to nearly all of them by 2018. Those systems were built with HIPAA compliance as a design requirement, and HIPAA became a ready justification for withholding records, including for treatment disclosures the Privacy Rule permits without patient authorization. Sharing across institutions lagged so far behind adoption that Congress prohibited information blocking in the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, and federal officials still describe the practice as widespread. The rules meant to protect data helped entrench the silos that now limit what any system, including AI, can learn from them.

Patient Choice Moves Data Outside the Boundary

Patients’ own decisions also move health information across HIPAA’s boundary. HIPAA’s right of access allows a patient to direct a covered entity to transmit records to any application the patient designates. Per HHS guidance, once data reach an unassociated third-party application selected by the patient, HIPAA protections no longer apply. Thus, the copy of a laboratory result held in a hospital portal remains protected, while the copy delivered to a consumer application is not. Protection depends on an act of consumer election instead of on the sensitivity of the information, and few consumers realize that they are making such a choice.

Federal access policy has substantially increased the volume of this flow. The information blocking rule requires certified systems to expose standardized interfaces and prohibits providers from screening the applications that patients choose. Concurrently, the volume of records exchanged through the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) grew from 10 million to more than one billion in under a year, and its adoption of standardized, machine-readable exchange renders clinical data usable by any tool that receives it. Federal payment policy is beginning to harness that speed: CMS’s prior authorization rule requires payers in Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, and the exchanges to automate prior authorization through the same standardized interfaces by 2027, with faster decision deadlines in force since January 2026.

This dynamic creates a paradox within the access agenda. As the authors have noted in prior work, expanded patient access to medical records is a meaningful policy achievement that patients deserve. Yet the same infrastructure is also the largest single mechanism moving health data beyond the reach of health-specific regulation. The goal of expanded access remains sound, and its consequences now warrant governance.

Classification Challenges for AI Intermediaries

Deployment Paths

Consider a tool that reads a clinical note and rewrites it in plain language for the patient.

- Hospital deployment (vendor): The vendor supplying it operates as a business associate under HIPAA.

- Hospital deployment (in-house): A tool the hospital builds in-house is subject to governance simply as part of the hospital’s own operations.

- Patient selection: When a patient selects the same tool and supplies records through an access request, the tool operates as a consumer application outside HIPAA.

- Clinic offering with patient data: When the tool is offered through a clinic but processes patient-supplied data, its status is genuinely unclear.

The tool’s function is identical in each case; only the deployment path differs.

Definition Difficulties

Without regulatory definitions, health system counsel cannot classify tools, so health systems are unlikely to deploy them. This ambiguity does not merely slow adoption; it also shapes which tools are built in the first place.

Notably, the federal government’s own resource for determining which rules apply to a health application is an interactive tool that walks developers through FTC, HHS, and FDA regimes. The need for a multiagency decision tree illustrates the complexity that both developers and health systems currently face.

Consequences of Misclassification

At the same time, the consequences of misclassification are increasing on only one side of the boundary. The 2026 escalation of information blocking enforcement, which included announced referrals to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, the Office of Inspector General, and the Department of Justice, increases the penalties for failing to share data while adding no clarity regarding the obligations of the tools that receive it. Rising compliance stakes without corresponding regulatory clarity tends to favor established entities, which can absorb legal uncertainty, over new entrants, which generally cannot.

Regulatory Avoidance by Design

Ultimately, the regulatory boundary has become a design choice. To place its product outside the HIPAA-regulated space, a company can take these three steps:

- Frame its product as wellness rather than medicine.

- Obtain data from patients, not providers.

- Accept payment from consumers instead of insurers.

Companies make this choice rationally and, as discussed below, it is frequently the only economically viable option. However, a system in which product architecture determines the applicable regulator inverts the logic of public accountability, as the entities holding sensitive information about large populations increasingly operate under the least health-specific oversight.

Approach of the FDA

The FDA classifies the same tools by a different logic. The agency does not regulate AI as such; it regulates products that meet the statutory definition of a device, and it scales oversight to what a function does and to the consequence of relying on an incorrect output. In an August 2026 discussion paper on generative AI devices, the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH) proposes a two-axis framework of activity and consequences. The activity axis runs from informational functions, which either present information or direct the user toward an action, to action-taking functions, which act either under clinician supervision or autonomously. The consequences axis grades the severity of harm an error would cause.

HIPAA asks who holds the data; FDA asks what the software does with them. The same plain-language tool can therefore be a business associate under one regime and fall outside device review under the other, and neither determination informs the other.

Interpretation Versus Practice

State law introduces a parallel question that federal classification cannot answer. Texas defines the practice of medicine as the diagnosis or treatment of a mental or physical disease or disorder, an activity reserved to licensed providers. An AI tool that interprets an individual’s health data and renders a personalized assessment approaches that definition, yet no state has said where interpretation ends and practice begins. Developers manage the uncertainty with disclaimers stating that their products do not provide medical advice, which leaves the question with consumers. That strategy is now under federal scrutiny. CDRH’s discussion paper states that the agency is considering whether a patient-facing informational function becomes any less directive because it includes a “talk to your doctor” statement, and whether directiveness depends on the substance and context of an output rather than on hedging words such as “consider” or “should.”

Health Data Economy Outside HIPAA

Federal Policy Is Expanding the Unregulated Space

The space outside HIPAA’s boundary is where growth is concentrated and federal policy is accelerating that growth. The HHS secretary has spoken of his vision “that every American is wearing a wearable within four years,” supported by one of the largest advertising campaigns in the department’s history. CMS has convened more than 60 technology and healthcare companies, including electronic health record (EHR) vendors and wearable manufacturers, into a voluntary Health Technology Ecosystem for consumer-facing digital health tools, largely assembled beyond HIPAA’s perimeter.

Additionally, in January 2026, the FDA revised its General Wellness policy such that noninvasive trackers of physiologic parameters, including blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and glucose trends, may qualify as unregulated wellness products, provided they avoid disease claims. Accordingly, wellness framing now functions as an explicit compliance strategy with regulatory endorsement.

Figure 1 illustrates the expanding landscape of healthcare, in which regulated healthcare sits at the center. Each ring marks a federal action since 2021 that enlarged, or acknowledged the growth of, the space outside HIPAA’s boundary:

- 2021 — FTC policy statement: FTC interprets the Health Breach Notification Rule to reach health applications and connected devices.

- 2024 — Health Breach Notification Rule amendment: Codifies that interpretation; enforcement remains case by case and after harm occurs.

- 2025 — Health Savings Account (HSA) eligibility expansion: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act extends health savings accounts to lower-premium marketplace plan enrollees, effective Jan. 1, 2026.

- January 2026 — FDA general wellness revision: Noninvasive physiologic trackers may qualify as unregulated wellness products if they avoid disease claims.

- 2026 and beyond — HHS wearables initiative: HHS campaign for universal wearable adoption and a CMS ecosystem of consumer digital health tools, largely outside HIPAA.

The two FTC actions are the consumer regulator’s response to a space that had already outgrown health-specific oversight; the outer three rings are policy choices that enlarge it further.

Figure 1 — The Expanding Landscape of Healthcare

HIPAA’s boundary is being redrawn from both directions. Seven months after loosening the wellness exemption, CDRH released a discussion paper on what oversight of generative AI devices would require, from premarket benchmarking of safety and clinical proficiency to postmarket monitoring for performance drift. These two moves point in different directions: fewer products inside device review, and heavier expectations for those that remain. A developer deciding which side of the line to build on now has a clearer view of the cost of being inside it.

Consumers Receive Less Than They Expect

Perception Gap

What consumers receive outside the boundary is systematically more limited than they generally believe. A widely used smartwatch screens for atrial fibrillation but not for the many other cardiac events associated with similar symptoms; therefore, the absence of an alert indicates little about what the device does not assess. Disclaimers explaining these limitations exist but are rarely read, while the sense of reassurance is immediate. Similarly, menstrual and fertility tracking applications are frequently understood as clinical instruments when they largely function as calendars with predictive layers. Because the information these applications collect falls outside HIPAA, it may be shared with or sold to third parties in ways the Privacy Rule would prohibit for a covered entity holding identical data, a practice the FTC enforcement actions discussed below illustrate.

The gap between what a device measures and what its buyers believe it measures has reached the courts. In August 2026, a proposed class action filed in federal court in California alleged that a leading smart ring, marketed as tracking sleep stages with near-clinical accuracy, lacks the sensors that clinical sleep staging requires and instead generates estimates from heart rate, movement, and temperature. The allegations are untested. The complaint nonetheless illustrates the structure of the problem: The product is sold in the language of measurement, the consumer pays for the device and then for a subscription to interpret it, and the remedy, if any, runs through consumer fraud law rather than through any health regulator.

Uneven Benefit

Whatever benefit wearables confer, it accrues unevenly. In a nationally representative survey, 18% of adults with established cardiovascular disease and 26% of those at risk for it reported using a wearable, compared with 29% of the general population, and older age, lower education, and lower income each predicted lower use. The people the HHS secretary hopes to reach are the least likely to be wearing a device, and the population whose data trains these products skews toward those who can afford them.

Conversational AI

Conversational AI is the newest intermediary and the least defined. A consumer who describes symptoms to a chatbot receives information that can shift, within a single exchange, from general education to a specific instruction. CDRH acknowledged exactly this dynamic in its August 2026 discussion paper: A conversational device may begin by performing an informational function and migrate to an action-directing one, so the CDRH is considering assessing risk across realistic conversational trajectories instead of one function at a time. The paper also treats errors in both directions as harm: 1) underescalation, which delays treatment, and 2) overescalation, which leads to unnecessary resource utilization and erodes trust. The paper is a request for feedback, not policy, and it applies only to tools that meet the statutory definition of a device. Most consumer chatbots are designed to avoid that definition, so their oversight defaults to the FTC and its consumer protection rules.

States’ Involvement

States have begun to respond to the protection gaps described above. Washington’s My Health My Data Act is the first law in the country to protect health data falling outside HIPAA and is enforceable through a private right of action. A state-level patchwork is presently forming, so whether a consumer’s health data receives any protection depends on the state in which they live.

State law also faces a jurisdictional problem that any state-level remedy must confront. Health data do not stay where they are generated; consumer applications route information to cloud data centers and backup sites in other states and other countries. A national company would need to identify which users are residents of each state that has enacted such a law and apply that state’s rules to their data wherever they are stored; whether these protections follow a resident who travels or a former resident who moves remains untested. A state can legislate for its residents, but it cannot inspect a server abroad. This limit is one reason the federal baseline proposed below matters, and it is why this brief’s Texas recommendations rely on the state’s authority as purchaser and funder as opposed to a new privacy statute.

Tax Policy Subsidizes Data Collection

Tax policy has further expanded this space. The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act substantially expanded eligibility for HSAs, extending them as of January 2026 to enrollees in lower-premium marketplace plans who were previously ineligible. At the same time, a retail infrastructure now exists to process wearable purchases through pretax dollars, with letters of medical necessity generated at checkout to satisfy the Internal Revenue Service’s qualified medical expense standard. In effect, pretax subsidy is expanding what qualifies as a healthcare-related item, while the data those items collect carry no health-specific protection.

FTC Serves as the Default Regulator

Oversight of this economy defaults to the FTC, which acts only after harm has occurred. In 2021, the FTC stated that the Health Breach Notification Rule already covered consumer health applications, a policy interpretation it codified by amendment in 2024. The rule produced its first enforcement action against GoodRx in 2023 for sharing users’ medication data with advertising platforms, followed by an action against Premom for disclosing fertility data to third-party analytics firms. Separately, BetterHelp paid $7.8 million under the FTC’s general deception authority for disclosing mental health intake data to advertisers.

The pattern across these actions is consistent: Enforcement proceeds case by case and after harm has occurred, binds only the defendant, and establishes no prospective standards. Notably, the same category of data breach triggers a comprehensive regulatory response inside a hospital but only breach notification and fines when it occurs within a consumer application.

Patients Do Not Share in the Value of Their Data

One further discrepancy warrants attention. AI models are increasingly trained on patient data drawn from both sides of HIPAA’s boundary, yet the value those models generate does not return to the patients whose information enabled them. No current framework requires that patients be notified, included, or compensated when their records contribute to training data. Patients thus supply the most valuable input in health AI development without participating in its returns, a dynamic that compounds the Baker Institute Center for Health Policy’s (CHP) finding that patients remain among the system’s least well-served participants.

“If you are not paying for something, you’re not the customer; you’re the product being sold.” Widely attributed to Andrew Lewis in a 2010 observation about Google and its users, this line described an advertising economy in which free services were financed by the audience’s attention and data. Health wearables have inverted even that arrangement. The consumer pays for the device, then pays a subscription to have their own physiology interpreted back to them, while the company typically reserves the right under its terms of use to apply the same data to product development and model training. The user pays to be the product.

Consumer Technology in Clinical Research

This consumer device ecosystem has also been used for population-scale clinical research. A landmark atrial fibrillation study reached 419,297 participants through consumer hardware and remote physicians. The study was run by licensed physicians under research oversight but was unprecedented in that a consumer technology company generated the clinical data and reached a population that no health system alone could have accessed. The same ecosystem that under-protects consumers can, under research oversight, produce evidence at a scale no clinic could assemble, which suggests the problem is governance rather than the devices themselves.

Economic Incentives Shape Where AI Is Deployed

Investment Concentrates Where AI Protects Revenue

Examining where health AI is purchased clarifies the boundary’s practical logic. Inside HIPAA’s boundary, the direct purchasers of data tools are health systems and insurers, on the expectation that better health and lower cost will reach patients downstream. The two purchasers have opposing financial drivers:

- Payers succeed when they avoid paying for care, so they deploy AI to accelerate prior authorization and claims determinations.

- Hospitals succeed when they are reimbursed for services, so they deploy AI toward billing and denial management.

Each side invests in systems that protect its revenue against the other. Investment therefore concentrates where AI defends an institutional balance sheet rather than where it improves patient understanding or clinical outcomes.

Patient-facing tools have no comparable purchaser. As the authors’ prior work established, no reimbursement code, quality bonus, or contractual term currently pays any party when a patient understands their care or when a consumer tool correctly connects a symptom to the right care. A developer building for patients therefore builds a consumer product, priced for individuals and architected outside HIPAA’s perimeter, where regulatory oversight is thinnest. Developers thus resolve the classification ambiguity described above by avoiding the regulated space rather than by complying with its rules. The same margin logic stratifies adoption geographically: Rural systems operating on narrow margins can generally only afford documentation assistance over more substantial clinical tools, so the communities with the greatest needs receive the least capable technology.

Fragmented Data Limits What AI Can Learn

One possible solution would be to transmit raw wearable and application data into the medical record, although clinicians have reasonable grounds for resisting it:

- Electronic health records were not designed to manage continuous streams of consumer data.

- Clinical care is fragmented, so no one is responsible for integrating those data into a plan.

- No payment mechanism covers the clinician time required to review them.

- Unassigned data typically become unreviewed data.

Functional counter-models already exist at smaller scales, for example:

- A cardiologist prescribes a connected blood pressure cuff, sets patient-specific parameters, and receives an alert only when readings fall outside them.

- An endocrinologist reviews a patient’s continuous glucose data at scheduled visits.

These arrangements work because responsibility for the data stream is explicitly assigned. Policy should aim to reproduce that assignment instead of mandating undifferentiated data transfer

The separation between HIPAA-covered clinical records and consumer-generated health data also constrains what AI systems can learn. Training data drawn solely from wearables can be unreliable, as sensor validity varies, self-reported logging tends to decline after initial use, and the absence of recorded data is frequently mistaken for the absence of symptoms. Training data drawn solely from EHRs capture clinical encounters but omit the periods between them. Because combining the two sources at scale requires authorization or de-identification pathways that are administratively burdensome and rarely pursued, models trained on either source reflect systematically incomplete pictures of the same individuals. Questions of ownership compound this limitation, as it remains unresolved whether a model trained on one health system’s records may be deployed elsewhere, and through what channels the resulting value flows.

Voluntary Oversight Challenges

Evaluation standards remain largely voluntary as well. The FDA’s predetermined change control framework addresses how regulated AI-enabled devices may be updated without a new marketing submission, which is a meaningful advance. However, most language model tools that process health information never enter device review at all. CDRH’s August 2026 discussion paper proposes a competency-based approach for generative AI devices, benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation, modeled on how clinicians are credentialed. It also lists clinicians, healthcare institutions, payers, professional societies, standards bodies, and state authorities as sharing responsibility for postmarket oversight, and asks how those roles can be structured without diffusing manufacturer accountability. That question is the right one, and it applies with more force outside device review than inside it. Responsibility that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. The phased evidentiary standards that medicine requires for pharmaceuticals remain optional for algorithms that increasingly mediate care.

Reimbursement Codes as Boundary Enforcement

Ultimately, the most consequential boundary enforcement is fiscal. The AI services that have earned billing codes generally produce a diagnostic result a provider can charge for, such as autonomous screening for diabetic retinopathy. Other important outcomes, such as enabling patient comprehension, produce no such result and have no corresponding code, so tools built to address them have no purchaser inside the regulated system. With substantial private investment available outside the HIPAA boundary, the payment vacuum polices the perimeter more effectively than any regulator does. Tools that cannot be reimbursed within the system will continue to be built outside it until the underlying incentives change. Regulation, meanwhile, is beginning to ask for what payment does not fund: CDRH’s discussion paper lists communication quality and user comprehension among the elements it would benchmark before authorizing a generative AI device, including whether users across health literacy levels can understand an output and its limits.

Policy Recommendations

The recommendations below reflect CHP’s approach to health technology: Regulation should focus on the functions performed and outcomes achieved rather than on restricting market entrants. The objective is a boundary determined by policy instead of product architecture, with obligations that follow health data wherever they travel and a market that remains accessible to the developers most likely to serve patients.

1. Clarify the Classification of AI Intermediaries

HHS should issue definitive classification guidance for AI tools that handle clinical data, stating with concrete examples when such tools operate as business associates, when they operate as consumer applications, and what duties apply in each circumstance. The guidance should establish a safe and attestable pathway for patient-authorized tools so that a patient’s decision to use a translation or organization tool does not eliminate protections entirely. Clarity, not additional stringency, is what both patient safety and market access presently require.

2. Modernize the Statutory Definition of Regulated Health Activity

Congress should update the statutory definition of regulated health activity. HIPAA’s reliance on biller identity was appropriate for administrative simplification in 1996, but it cannot adequately govern an economy in which sensitive health inferences are generated by unlicensed entities that bill no one. Baseline privacy, security, and disclosure obligations should follow the function performed and the sensitivity of the data. Such a baseline, which states would remain free to exceed, would impose obligations before data are disclosed rather than only requiring notice afterward, as the Health Breach Notification Rule currently does, and it would ensure that a consumer's protections do not depend on the state in which they live.

3. Coordinate Federal Oversight and Condition Tax Subsidies on Disclosure

HHS and the FTC should formalize referral and joint-guidance mechanisms covering consumer health data so that the gap between the two regimes is narrowed. Additionally, devices purchased with tax-advantaged health dollars should carry plain-language disclosure of their data practices at the point of sale. Where public subsidy supports the purchase of data-collecting devices, consumers can reasonably expect to be informed about what those devices collect and where that information is transmitted.

4. Establish Texas Standards for AI Tools and Health Data

A federal baseline leaves room for states to act, and Texas can move on three fronts identified in this brief: 1) the unsettled line between interpretation and the practice of medicine, 2) the state’s position as a purchaser of AI-processed data through Medicaid managed care, and 3) the rural margin gap that keeps accountable monitoring from spreading. The second and third items require no new privacy statute; they use the state’s authority as purchaser and funder, which sidesteps the jurisdictional limits that constrain state privacy law.

Clarify interpretation versus practice: The Legislature and the Texas Medical Board should clarify when AI interpretation of health data for Texans constitutes the practice of medicine and when disclosure obligations are sufficient, a clarification that would protect patients without creating entry barriers that only established firms could satisfy.

Set contractual standards: The Texas Health and Human Services Commission should establish contract standards for AI tools that process Medicaid enrollee data regardless of those tools’ HIPAA status, including transparency, security, and human review requirements.

Address rural funding: The state’s rural health investments should fund accountable remote-monitoring programs, in which prescribed devices operate with clinician-set parameters and reimbursement covers the clinician time required to review and act on the resulting data. Rural systems generally lack the operating margin to absorb that review cost, which is a principal reason the model has spread unevenly. Directing state funds toward monitoring and clinician capacity, rather than toward devices alone, would extend to rural Texans the accountable data integration that better-resourced systems already provide.

Governing the Boundary of Healthcare

Research from CHP has established that patients have gained access to their health information but overwhelmingly do not have the ability to understand it. This brief addresses a related finding: The tools, devices, and platforms that increasingly interpret Americans’ health information operate largely beyond the boundary of health regulation. That boundary was drawn three decades ago around billing relationships and is now enforced primarily through what payment systems will and will not support.

Consumers generally cannot identify where the boundary falls, developers select which side of it to occupy, and the health data that patients generate contribute to models and markets that return no value to them. Health policy should now address not only how to protect medical records, but also what qualifies as healthcare and which entities are accountable for it. Currently shaped by product design decisions, that determination belongs in public policy, where both Texas and the federal government can take the lead.

review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
